newsitem.title: Philippines: Philippines bars activists ahead of APEC meeting.
newsitem.headline: Philippines bars activists ahead of APEC meeting.

text.p: The Philippines barred five Sri Lankan activists from entering the country, after organisers of next week's APEC summit said on Sunday Philippine leftists were planning to incite violence during the 18-nation meeting.

The five arrived at Manila airport on Saturday to attend a meeting of non-governmental organisations in protest at Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), which is aimed at promoting economic cooperation on trade and investment.
President Fidel Ramos's government said it would bar any foreigners, who authorities fear could cause trouble, during the November 25 summit in Subic, north of Manila.

U.S. President Bill Clinton will attend the summit, where he was due to meet Asian heavy weights such as Chinese President Jiang Zemin, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-Sam.

Some 400 business executives will meet the leaders in Manila on November 24 and APEC is expected to formally adopt private sector recommendations, such as a programme to help tackle the region's massive infrastructure needs.
Leftist groups plan to organise "protest caravans" from Manila to Subic to coincide with the event. A total of 15 foreign delegates to anti-APEC meetings have been barred in the past month.
Manila has refused to give a visa to Nobel Peace laureate and self-exiled East Timor independence leader, Jose Ramos-Horta, saying his presence could be disruptive.
Leaders of 16 of the 18 APEC members are expected to attend, including Indonesian President Suharto, whose country invaded East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year.
The move has never been accepted by the United Nations.

Romeo Royandoyan, secretary general of the Manila People's Forum on APEC to be held in parallel with the summit, said the banning of the Sri Lankans showed "government paranoia about security." The Forum meeting is to be attended by academics, peace activists and environmentalists.
Royandoyan said the barred Sri Lankan group was led by Anton Marcus, the president of an industrial transport and workers union in Sri Lanka.
Lisandro Abadia, the Philippines organising committee director-general, said Philippine left-wing protesters were more likley to cause trouble than foreign extremists.

"What I heard is these hard-headed people will not go to designated demonstration areas but their plan is to foul-bait, taunt our law enforcers," Abadia, the former Philippines armed forces chief, said in a radio interview.
"That's why my instruction to law enforcers is don't be intimidated by these people, don't be provoked...we really must keep our cool," Abadia said.

Manila Mayor Alfredo Lim, speaking in the same interview, said leftist groups were bent on creating "a happening" to embarrass the government. Leftists dismissed as government propaganda accusations they planned to make trouble.
